```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.5,
                      out.width = "100%", dpi = 110)
```

```{r setup}
library(sdidlab)
panel <- prop99_panel()
```

synthdid's `sc_estimate()` is a synthetic control matched on pre-period
outcomes. `fit_scm()` is the classic Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010)
estimator: it matches on a predictor matrix with predictor weights `V`, and
adds the Abadie-L'Hour bias correction and penalty. Use it through
`fit_spec()` with `estimator = "scm"`, or directly on a matrix.

## The estimator

Donor weights `w` lie on the simplex and minimise the `V`-weighted
discrepancy between the treated unit's predictors and the weighted donors'.
By default the predictors are the pre-period outcomes, standardised, with
equal weights. `v_method = "mspe"` searches for the `V` that best fits the
pre-period outcome, as `Synth` does.

The weights are solved exactly by an active-set method. The test suite checks
them against the optimality conditions of the problem and against `Synth`.

```{r}
setup <- build_setup(sdid_spec(), panel)
fit <- fit_scm(setup$Y, setup$N0, setup$T0, bias_correct = FALSE)
round(sort(fit$omega[fit$omega > 0], decreasing = TRUE), 3)
fit$att
```

## Bias correction

Even a good synthetic control leaves some discrepancy in the predictors, and
that discrepancy biases the estimate. The Abadie-L'Hour correction regresses
the outcome on the predictors among the donors, one period at a time, and
subtracts the model's prediction of the leftover discrepancy:

```{r}
fit_bc <- suppressMessages(fit_scm(setup$Y, setup$N0, setup$T0))
c(uncorrected = fit$att, corrected = fit_bc$att)
```

One consequence is easy to misread. **In any period used as a predictor, the
corrected gap is mechanically near zero**, because that period's regression
fits it almost exactly. Flat pre-period gaps after correction confirm that
the correction ran; they are not evidence of a perfect match. That is why
sdidlab's SCM figures show the *uncorrected* gap as the measure of fit.

## Exact fits, and the penalty

When the treated unit's predictors lie inside the donors' convex hull, the
synthetic control can match them **exactly**. Many different weightings then
fit equally well, and they imply different counterfactuals, so the estimate
depends on which one the solver happens to return. It is not identified by
the data. sdidlab flags this (`exact_match`) and warns. When the whole
pre-period is reproduced exactly (`exact_fit`), it also leaves the RMSPE
ratio undefined, rather than letting a near-zero denominator rank the unit
first in a permutation test.

Matching on only three pre-periods makes this easy to see:

```{r}
exact <- fit_scm(setup$Y, setup$N0, setup$T0, outcome_periods = c(5, 12, 19),
                 bias_correct = FALSE)
c(exact_match = exact$exact_match, exact_fit = exact$exact_fit)
```

The Abadie and L'Hour (2021) penalty resolves it. Adding
`penalty * sum_j w_j ||X_1 - X_j||^2` to the objective charges for using
donors that are individually far from the treated unit. For any positive
value the weights are unique. A small penalty picks, among the exact fits,
the one built from the nearest donors:

```{r}
penalised <- fit_scm(setup$Y, setup$N0, setup$T0, outcome_periods = c(5, 12, 19),
                     bias_correct = FALSE, penalty = 1e-3)
c(unpenalised = exact$att, penalised = penalised$att)
```

Larger penalties trade pre-period fit for locality. As the penalty grows, the
synthetic control becomes the single nearest donor.

## Permutation inference

The Abadie-style test refits the synthetic control with each donor in turn
standing in as the treated unit, with the real treated unit removed from its
pool, and ranks the treated unit's ratio of post-period to pre-period RMSPE
against the placebos'. Through `fit_spec()` this happens automatically:

```{r}
run <- suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(fit_spec(sdid_spec(estimator = "scm"), panel)))
c(att = run$fit$att, p = run$fit$rmspe_p, rank = run$fit$rmspe_rank, of = run$fit$placebos_total)
```

```{r}
plot_scm_gaps(run)
```

The smallest p-value attainable is one over the number of units: here
`r round(1 / run$fit$placebos_total, 3)`. Read it as a rank, not as a
continuous p-value.

`rmspe_pvalue()` also supports one-sided tests, which regain some power with
few donors when the direction of the effect is known in advance.
